item.title: Normative functional network localization of gray matter alterations in idiopathic generalized epilepsy.
item.description:
Frontiers in neurology
Objective Idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) has traditionally been considered a non-lesional epilepsy syndrome on conventional MRI, yet voxel-based morphometry (VBM) studies have reported subtle gray matter (GM) abnormalities across diverse brain regions. These findings remain spatially heterogeneous and difficult to reconcile. We aimed to characterize the normative functional connectivity patterns associated with reported GM alterations in IGE using functional connectivity network mapping (FCNM), and to explore whether these spatially heterogeneous findings show a reproducible pattern of observed network overlap. Methods We systematically identified 18 whole-brain VBM studies of IGE, including 111 reported peak coordinates from 1,492 participants. Coordinates reflecting both increased and decreased GM were pooled in the primary analysis to characterize normative connectivity patterns associated with reported GM alterations irrespective of alteration direction. Using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data from a normative discovery cohort (Human Connectome Project, N = 1,093), we mapped the functional connectivity of these GM coordinates to identify a convergent IGE-related network. The reproducibility of the observed spatial pattern was explored using an independent, cross-scanner validation cohort (Southwest University Adult Lifespan Dataset, N = 329) and two alternative seed sizes (1-mm and 7-mm radii). Results Reported GM alterations in IGE were associated with an observed distributed normative functional connectivity pattern involving the bilateral middle temporal gyri, bilateral thalami, left superior frontal gyrus, and right putamen. In the HCP discovery analysis, this network showed the greatest observed overlap with the subcortical network (overlap proportion = 42.77%) and secondary correspondence with the default mode network (DMN; overlap proportion = 11.06%). Analysis using the independent SALD connectome showed a similar descriptive pattern, with the greatest observed overlap again involving the subcortical network (overlap proportion = 43.98%), whereas DMN correspondence was weaker. Conclusion Reported GM alterations in IGE converge most robustly onto a subcortical normative functional network involving the thalamus and putamen, with additional DMN involvement observed primarily in the HCP discovery analysis. These findings provide preliminary, descriptive evidence that reported GM alterations in IGE are associated with a reproducible subcortical normative connectivity pattern across two connectome datasets, although the available analyses do not establish above-chance or disease-specific network convergence.

item.title: Two clusters of brain regions with distinct age-related profiles of functional connectivity in autism spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Brain functional connectivity changes throughout development, and individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may follow trajectories that differ from those of typically developing controls. Using large multisite resting-state fMRI cross-sectional datasets, we examined how functional connectivity differences between ASD and typically developing controls change across a broad age range of 5 to 64 y. A data-driven analysis identified two spatially distributed clusters of cortical regions showing distinct age-related profiles of ASD-TD connectivity differences. Cluster 1 was marked by consistent hypoconnectivity across ages, suggesting a stable neural signature of ASD. Cluster 2 was characterized by hypoconnectivity in childhood that gradually diminished with age, suggesting a temporary delay profile. These clusters were systematically organized along the sensory-association axis. Cluster 1 mainly involved lower-rank sensory and sensorimotor cortices, while Cluster 2 mainly involved higher-rank association cortices. Brain-behavior analyses revealed greater and broader ASD symptom associations across ages in the consistent hypoconnectivity profile than the delay profile. Further subtype analyses suggested that social-affect symptoms were associated with greater hypoconnectivity than repetitive behavior symptoms in both clusters. Spatial correlation analyses with neurotransmitter maps revealed associations of Cluster 1 with mGluR5 and of Cluster 2 with GABAA α5, providing insight into the neurobiological basis of the two clusters. In a cross-disorder validation analysis, applying the same analytic framework to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder did not reveal comparable results. Together, these findings suggest that ASD-related functional connectivity alterations are developmentally heterogeneous and organized along the cortical hierarchy, providing a developmental perspective for understanding the neurobiology of ASD.

item.title: Uncovering Latent Cognitive, Metacognitive, and Neural Bases of Problem-Solving Deficits in Children with Developmental Dyscalculia.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Developmental dyscalculia (DD) affects 7-10% of children and is characterized by persistent difficulties in arithmetic problem-solving, which depends on the dynamic interplay between cognitive and metacognitive control processes governing strategy execution and selection. Conventional behavioral and neuroimaging approaches do not simultaneously quantify these latent processes and link them to distributed neural mechanisms, leaving the neurocognitive and metacognitive underpinnings of DD insufficiently characterized. We integrated Bayesian computational modeling with whole-brain decoding to uncover cognitive, metacognitive, and neural bases of problem-solving deficits in DD using a sample of 68 children aged 8-10 years (38 female). Children with DD showed deficits across all problem-solving strategies (counting, retrieval, and decomposition), indicating reduced strategy execution efficiency. They also exhibited significant metacognitive impairments: longer baseline switching times between strategies, reduced sensitivity to problem difficulty, and lower adaptivity in selecting optimal strategies. Whole-brain Elastic Net decoding accurately distinguished DD from TA peers based on distributed activation patterns across frontoparietal cortex, hippocampus, and ventral-visual regions, whereas univariate approaches did not. Linear multivariate brain-behavioral analyses and nonlinear transformer-based predictions converged in showing that these distributed signatures predicted counting efficiency and switching sensitivity. Notably, brain-behavior relations reversed in direction between groups, positive in TA children but negative in DD, most strikingly in the hippocampus. These findings demonstrate that arithmetic difficulties in DD arise from deficits in both strategy execution efficiency and metacognitive control, reflecting an altered mapping between distributed neural activity, and highlight the power of integrating computational modeling with brain-wide decoding to understand learning disabilities.

item.title: Hemispheric Asymmetry of Neuroimaging Biomarkers in Early Onset Alzheimer's Disease: Clinical and Cognitive Outcomes.
item.description:
Annals of neurology
Objective Individuals diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease (AD) often exhibit amyloid, tau, and atrophy predominantly in the left or right hemisphere, but group-level analyses typically ignore inter-individual variability and changing asymmetry patterns when averaging data across participants in phenotypically diverse cohorts. Methods We examined left/right hemispheric asymmetry in amyloid positron emission tomography (PET), tau PET, and cortical atrophy in sporadic early-onset AD from 585 deeply phenotyped individuals across 2 cohorts to investigate its clinical correlates. For each imaging biomarker, we computed a global asymmetry index reflecting left/right hemisphere signal difference, and an analogous asymmetry value for PET/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) voxels. We examined clinical and cognitive correlates of this asymmetry across phenotypes cross-sectionally and longitudinally in a subset of 218 participants. Results Both left and right asymmetry were common for all clinical phenotypes and was correlated between imaging biomarkers. Asymmetry patterns varied spatially within phenotypes, and asymmetry in tau PET and MRI volumes was related to hemisphere-dependent cognitive deficits and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Longitudinal analyses revealed stable amyloid PET asymmetry, decreasing tau PET asymmetry, and increasing MRI volume asymmetry. Interpretation Hemispheric asymmetry is common in early onset AD and correlates with clinical outcomes. Our longitudinal findings suggest a time-lagged asymmetry peak in amyloid, then tau, then atrophy. Taken together, our results position asymmetry as an important feature of AD heterogeneity, as it provides insight into disease mechanisms and trajectories. ANN NEUROL 2026.

item.title: Default mode network mechanisms of trait rumination in treatment-resistant depression and rTMS: evidence from source-localized EEG.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Rumination is a transdiagnostic feature of multiple psychiatric disorders and is a critical risk factor for more severe episodes and poor treatment outcomes in treatment-resistant depression (TRD). Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) ameliorates both depressive and ruminative symptoms in TRD. While prior literature has linked rumination to abnormal default mode network (DMN) connectivity, the electrophysiological correlates of rumination in the DMN are not well understood. Methods Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) data were examined in a cohort of 66 TRD subjects who underwent 30 sessions of rTMS treatment for TRD administered to left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). We employed source-localization and calculated four metrics of functional connectivity (Amplitude Envelope Correlation [AEC], weighted Phase Lag Index [wPLI], magnitude-squared coherence, and Spectral Correlation Coefficient [SCC]) across five frequency bands within the DMN to identify the neural correlates of rumination in TRD. Correction for multiple comparisons was performed using the Network Based Statistic (NBS). Results Baseline severity of rumination and depression were positively correlated, but AEC alpha band connectivity was positively associated only with baseline rumination severity and not depression. Rumination severity prior to treatment was not associated with any other connectivity metric. Severity of rumination and depression decreased following rTMS treatment, but alpha AEC connectivity did not charge after 30 sessions of rTMS treatment. Conclusion Higher DMN connectivity, as measured by alpha-band AEC, is a stable trait-like neurophysiological marker of rumination that is not significantly affected by rTMS administered to left DLPFC.

item.title: Neural Circuits of Social Behavior in Autism Spectrum Disorder: From Mechanism to Intervention.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Introduction Difficulties in social communication and interaction are core diagnostic features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet interventions targeting these difficulties have modest and variable effects. Understanding mechanistically distinct contributions to social behaviors may identify new therapeutic opportunities. Methods This narrative review integrates human neuroimaging studies, supporting rodent circuit neuroscience, clinical intervention research, and developmental studies. We organize the findings into four overlapping functional-computational domains and relate these domains to the Research Domain Criteria Social Processes framework. Results The four domains are: (1) Social Reward and Social Interest, encompassing the incentive and hedonic value of social contact and motivation to engage; (2) Social Memory and Social-Affective Value, encompassing recognition of familiar individuals and learned affective or motivational associations; (3) Social Cue Perception, Action Representation, and Social Prediction/Timing, encompassing the processing and forecasting of dynamic social information; and (4) Higher-Order Social Cognition and Model Updating, encompassing mental-state inference and the updating of person-specific social models. Because these domains are not independent, interactions among reward, memory, cue processing, prediction, and higher-order inference create multiple possible developmental entry points, such that early differences in one process may alter experience-dependent learning in others. Evidence for specific causal cascades remains preliminary and requires longitudinal testing. Conclusions A circuit-and-development framework may improve hypothesis generation, domain-specific phenotyping, target-engagement assessment, and mechanism-aligned outcomes. Clinical translation, however, requires caution. Biomarkers should be validated as predictors of treatment response, cascade models should be tested longitudinally, and interventions should combine mechanism-informed targets with behavioral support that promotes generalization to daily life.

item.title: Altered frontal and dorsal hemodynamic engagement during mandarin aspiration processing in post-stroke aphasia: an fNIRS study.
item.description:
Brain and language
Auditory and speech-perception difficulties are common in post-stroke aphasia (PSA), but cortical responses during passive listening to Mandarin speech remain underexplored. Seventeen Mandarin-speaking individuals with PSA and 18 matched healthy controls listened to auditory oddball blocks containing /ba/ standards and /pa/ deviants during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Although these syllables instantiate an aspiration contrast strongly cued by voice onset time (VOT), standard and deviant trials were combined within a single block-level condition. The resulting measures therefore indexed activation during speech-containing blocks relative to silent inter-block intervals rather than phonemic discrimination, categorization, or VOT-specific processing. Seven theory-driven channels covering bilateral auditory, sensorimotor, inferior frontal, and dorsolateral prefrontal regions were analyzed using three HbO indices: β coefficient, peak amplitude, and temporal centroid. The PSA group showed an overall reduction in task-related HbO activation, reflected by a significant Group effect for the β coefficient. Peak amplitude also showed significant Group and Group × Channel effects, although no individual channel remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Temporal centroid showed no significant group or interaction effects. These findings provide preliminary evidence for reduced block-evoked cortical recruitment during passive auditory exposure to Mandarin speech sounds in PSA. Because the analysis did not include a direct standard-deviant or active auditory control comparison, the findings do not establish a selective impairment of phonemic discrimination, categorization, or VOT processing. Because patients were assessed 6-7 months after stroke onset, the activation differences may reflect both persistent impairment and recovery-related reorganization during the early chronic stage.

item.title: Neurovisceral model of social anxiety disorder: An integrative review.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Social anxiety involves persistent fear of negative evaluation that causes significant distress or avoidance in social situations and, when lasting at least six months with meaningful impairment across life domains, meets diagnostic criteria for social anxiety disorder (SAD). The origins and maintenance of SAD have been described by disparate models as dysregulation of central and peripheral networks involved in emotion regulation and threat appraisal. However, studies integrating central and peripheral levels of analysis remain scarce and lack integration, leaving our understanding of the neurobiology of SAD fragmented. Here we review these models and extant evidence. This review proposes an integrated neurovisceral model in which SAD reflects context-sensitive dysregulation among cortical regulation, limbic threat signaling, insular interoception, vagal and autonomic regulation, cardiac flexibility, HPA-axis output, and behavior. Genetic liability and behavioral inhibition are conceptualized as probabilistic influences on threat sensitivity and regulatory capacity. While environmental experience, developmental timing, sex-related factors, and stress sensitization shape the calibration of these systems. The model predicts heterogeneity along activation threshold, response magnitude, recovery, and central-peripheral coordination, which may give rise to acute hyperreactive, persistent sensitized/inflexible, and compromised/blunted SAD configurations. The model also generates testable predictions for longitudinal, multimodal research, and supports profile-sensitive approaches to assessment and treatment.

item.title: Excitation-Inhibition Balance and Fronto-Limbic Connectivity Distinguish TMS Treatment Outcomes in Refractory Depression.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is effective for treatment-resistant depression, but outcomes remain variable. The neurophysiological mechanisms underlying response remain poorly understood, limiting precision neuromodulation. Methods We combined transcranial magnetic stimulation with electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) and connectome-based Jansen-Rit neural mass modeling to investigate the mechanistic basis of treatment efficacy in 90 patients with treatment-resistant depression. Individualized whole-brain models were fitted to pre- and post-iTBS TMS-evoked potentials, yielding subject-specific estimates of synaptic connectivity, excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, and cortical dynamics. Brain states were defined by singular value decomposition of the model's population activity, and partial least squares analysis with nested cross-validation identified the brain-state pattern distinguishing responders from non-responders. Results We identified two neurophysiological signatures associated with treatment response. First, responders showed greater post-treatment reductions in 3-10 Hz oscillatory power, driven by shifts in E/I balance toward greater inhibitory control through reduced excitatory drive and increased inhibitory-to-pyramidal connectivity. Second, a pre-treatment brain state characterized by opposite-polarity dynamics between subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) and left DLPFC distinguished responders from non-responders, consistent with prior fMRI findings on frontolimbic anticorrelation. Neural trajectory analysis further revealed greater dynamical reorganization and increased attractor stability in responders following treatment. Conclusions These findings provide a neurophysiologically-informed framework linking iTBS treatment efficacy to specific changes in cortical E/I balance and frontolimbic circuit dynamics, pointing toward candidate markers that, with subject-specific structural connectivity and independent validation, may inform personalized neuromodulation approaches in treatment-resistant depression.

item.title: The role of white matter microstructure in the association between childhood maltreatment and adult post-traumatic symptoms.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a risk factor for adult post-traumatic symptoms and white matter (WM) alterations. It remains unknown how WM microstructure is affected alongside two common military conditions, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Data from 299 participants (53% male, 35.69 ± 12.23 years of age) of the Injury and Traumatic Stress (INTRuST) clinical consortium was analyzed. The study included 56 individuals with PTSD (41 with comorbid mTBI), 107 with mTBI, and 136 controls (no PTSD and/or mTBI). Diffusion parameters (mean, axial, and radial diffusivity, MD, AD, RD; fractional anisotropy, FA) in major WM tracts were extracted from diffusion MRI. CM was assessed using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ). Multiple regression models examined associations between CM severity and WM diffusion. Moderation analyses assessed the effect of PTSD and/or mTBI on these associations. Mediation analyses examined how WM diffusion affects the associations between CM and both PTSD and post-concussive symptom severity. Greater CM severity was associated with lower MD and AD, independent of PTSD and/or mTBI. WM diffusion, particularly in the corpus callosum and the superior longitudinal fasciculus, mediated the associations between CM severity and both PTSD (MD bab = 0.022, AD bab = 0.019-0.034) and post-concussive symptoms (MD bab = 0.028-0.040, AD bab = 0.032-0.047). Findings suggest that WM alterations are more strongly associated with CM itself than with either PTSD and/or mTBI. Mediating effects in regions critical for sensory integration highlight the role of WM microstructure as a neurobiological pathway through which CM might predispose to post-traumatic symptoms.

item.title: Mapping the psychosis spectrum - imaging neurosubtypes from multiscale functional network connectivity.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Psychosis exhibits marked neurobiological heterogeneity that is not adequately captured by symptom-based diagnoses. Although prior efforts have identified subgroups, it remains unclear how latent disease variability manifests within the brain's multiscale intrinsic functional organization and whether these patterns can be leveraged to systematically identify biologically driven subtypes of psychosis. Here, we aim to identify Psychosis Imaging Neurosubtypes (PINs)-homogeneous subgroups defined solely from neurobiological features of brain function, independent of clinical or cognitive definitions, and whether these subgroups show meaningful phenotypic differentiation. Resting-state fMRI data from 2103 B-SNIP 1&2 participants were used to compute subject-specific multiscale functional network connectivity (msFNC). We then derived a low-dimensional neurobiological subspace, termed Latent Network Connectivity, which captured system-wide interconnected multiscale information across three components. Projections of probands msFNC onto this subspace revealed three PINs through unsupervised learning that spanned DSM diagnoses (Schizophrenia, Bipolar, Schizoaffective Disorder). Although defined purely from intrinsic neurobiology, PINs exhibited distinct cognitive, clinical, and connectivity profiles. PIN-1, the most cognitively impaired, showed Cerebellar-Subcortical and Visual-Sensorimotor hypoconnectivity, alongside Visual-Subcortical hyperconnectivity. Most cognitively preserved PIN-2 showed Visual-Subcortical, Subcortical-Sensorimotor, and Subcortical-Higher Cognition hypoconnectivity. PIN-3 exhibited intermediate cognition, showing Cerebellar-Subcortical hypoconnectivity alongside Cerebellar-Sensorimotor and Subcortical-Sensorimotor hyperconnectivity. Although covariate-adjusted analyses did not reveal significant clinical differences among PINs, exploratory analyses identified selective differences in YMDR, PANSS, and Age of Onset. Notably, 55% of relatives aligned with the same neurosubtype as their probands, a rate significantly higher than chance and than DSM-based alignment, suggesting potential heritability. Cognitive performance reliably aligns with distinct brain connectivity patterns, which are also evident in relatives, supporting their construct validity. Our PINs partially converged with previously reported BSNIP Biotypes with some correspondence (e.g. PIN1 with Biotype 1) but not with the other Biotypes, which were determined using integrated electrophysiological, cognitive, and oculomotor data, supporting convergent validity, while also indicating that intrinsic rsfMRI derived multiscale connectivity partitions psychosis heterogeneity somewhat differently from multimodal biomarker approaches. These findings underscore the limitations of DSM-based classifications in capturing the biological complexity of psychotic disorders and highlight the potential of imaging-based neurosubtypes to enhance our understanding of the psychosis spectrum.
